claims.text: PdCuPtNiCo nanoparticles can initially form a near-equimolar, homogeneous single-phase solid solution with uniform elemental distribution.
Structural and chemical stability from 473 to 1923 K is governed by a balance between configurational entropy and temperature-driven atomic diffusion.
Configurational entropy favors an equimolar distribution in the HEA bulk.
Configurational entropy by itself stabilizes a homogeneous solid-solution state throughout the nanoparticle.
Cu has relatively low cohesive contribution and energetically unfavorable metallic bonding, which drives Cu toward the surface.
Pd's cohesive and surface energies, together with its bulk abundance, contribute to Pd surface segregation.
If atomic diffusion remains slower than the temperature increase, the solid-solution phase is maintained.
Thermal activation of diffusion eventually overcomes entropy stabilization and produces surface segregation and phase separation.
At low to moderate temperatures, sluggish atomic mobility maintains the solid-solution state.
Annealing can produce pronounced Cu and Pd segregation at the HEA surface.
Cu and Pd segregation changes the surface elemental composition and atomic configuration.
Surface segregation changes catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
A gradual temperature ramp from 473 to 1923 K will largely preserve the solid solution and cause only minor segregation.
Rapid or prolonged high-temperature exposure will produce more pronounced Cu and Pd segregation than a gradual ramp.
The prediction applies when reactive atmospheres and mechanical stresses are minimized.
Exceeding a critical temperature-time threshold at which diffusion is no longer kinetically limited causes significant phase separation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says the solid solution is maintained when diffusion is slower than the temperature increase, which would most naturally favor rapid heating. The predicted outcome instead assigns greater segregation to rapid exposure and greater retention to gradual heating, reversing the stated rate logic without an additional hold-time or equilibration argument.
